title: The external eye and eyelids
summary: What you see when you look someone in the eye: iris, pupil, sclera, conjunctiva, the corners of the eye, and the layered eyelid.
objectives: Identify the pupil, iris, sclera, eyebrow, eyelashes, eyelids, commissures and lacrimal caruncle
Describe the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva and the conjunctival fornices
List the layers of an eyelid from skin to conjunctiva
Name the muscles that open and close the eye
takeaways: The pupil is the opening in the centre of the coloured iris; the sclera is the white of the eye.
Conjunctiva: bulbar over the sclera, palpebral lining the lids, meeting at the superior and inferior fornices.
The lids meet at the medial and lateral commissures (canthi); the lacrimal caruncle sits at the medial one.
Eyelid layers: skin, areolar tissue, orbicularis oculi, tarsal plate with tarsal (meibomian) glands, palpebral conjunctiva.
Levator palpebrae superioris (with the smooth superior tarsal muscle) raises the upper lid; orbicularis oculi closes the eye.

steps.title: Iris, pupil and sclera
steps.text:
The coloured ring is the iris; the black hole in its centre is the pupil, which lets light into the eye. Around the iris lies the sclera, the tough white of the eye, and in front of the iris the clear cornea.

When small vessels on the front of the sclera dilate, the eye looks bloodshot.

check.q: What is the pupil?
check.a: The opening in the centre of the iris through which light enters.

steps.title: The conjunctiva
steps.text:
A thin, transparent mucous membrane - the conjunctiva - covers the white of the eye (bulbar conjunctiva) and lines the inner surface of the lids (palpebral conjunctiva). The two meet in deep recesses above and below the eye, the superior and inferior conjunctival fornices. It stops at the edge of the cornea.

Its inflammation, conjunctivitis ('pink eye'), makes the eye red and sticky.

check.q: Where do the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva meet?
check.a: At the superior and inferior conjunctival fornices.

steps.title: Brows, lashes and the corners of the eye
steps.text:
The eyebrows sit over the supraorbital ridge and shade the eye and divert sweat. The eyelids (palpebrae) and eyelashes keep particles out, and the closed lids cut out light during sleep. The gap between the lids is the palpebral fissure.

The lids meet at the medial and lateral commissures (canthi). The small pink mound at the medial commissure is the lacrimal caruncle.

check.q: What is found at the medial commissure?
check.a: The lacrimal caruncle.

steps.title: Layers of an eyelid
steps.text: From front to back an eyelid is: thin skin; loose areolar connective tissue; the orbicularis oculi muscle; a plate of dense connective tissue, the tarsal plate (superior and inferior tarsus), holding a row of tarsal (meibomian) glands that oil the lid margin; and finally the palpebral conjunctiva against the eye.
steps.clinical: A blocked tarsal gland swells into a painless lump in the lid, a chalazion.

check.q: List the layers of the eyelid from skin to eye.
check.a: Skin, areolar connective tissue, orbicularis oculi, tarsal plate with tarsal glands, palpebral conjunctiva.

steps.title: Opening and closing the eye
steps.text: Orbicularis oculi, a ring of skeletal muscle in the lids (facial nerve), closes the eye. The upper lid is raised by levator palpebrae superioris, which runs forward from the back of the orbit above the eye (oculomotor nerve). A thin sheet of smooth muscle, the superior tarsal muscle, inserts on the tarsal plate and gives a little extra lift under sympathetic control.
steps.clinical: Loss of the sympathetic supply (Horner syndrome) paralyses the superior tarsal muscle and gives a slight droop of the upper lid; an oculomotor palsy paralyses levator and gives a complete droop.

check.q: Which muscle raises the upper eyelid, and which closes the eye?
check.a: Levator palpebrae superioris (helped by the superior tarsal muscle) raises it; orbicularis oculi closes it.

practice.q: The conjunctiva lining the inner surface of the eyelids is the
practice.why: Bulbar conjunctiva covers the sclera; palpebral lines the lids.

practice.q: The lacrimal caruncle lies at the
practice.why: It is the pink mound in the medial corner of the eye.

practice.q: Tarsal (meibomian) glands are found in the
practice.why: They lie in a row within each tarsal plate and open on the lid margin.

practice.q: What makes an eye look bloodshot?
practice.a: Dilated blood vessels in the anterior sclera and overlying conjunctiva.

practice.q: What is the palpebral fissure?
practice.a: The opening between the upper and lower eyelids.

practice.q: Name the smooth muscle that inserts on the upper tarsal plate and its nerve supply.
practice.a: The superior tarsal muscle, supplied by sympathetic fibres.

title: Tears and the extrinsic eye muscles
summary: The route tears take from gland to nose, and the six muscles and three nerves that aim the eye.
objectives: Trace tears from the lacrimal gland to the nasal cavity
Name the six extrinsic eye muscles, the direction each turns the eye and its nerve
Explain what a smooth or jerky tracking test shows
takeaways: Lacrimal gland (superolateral) -> ducts -> across the eye -> lacrimal canaliculi -> lacrimal sac -> nasolacrimal duct -> nasal cavity.
Four recti turn the eye up, down, in and out; superior oblique turns it down and out, inferior oblique up and out.
LR6 SO4, rest 3: lateral rectus - abducens; superior oblique - trochlear; all others - oculomotor.
Tracking a moving target should be smooth; jerky tracking is abnormal.

steps.title: Where tears are made
steps.text: Tears are made by the lacrimal gland, tucked into the superolateral corner of the orbit above the eye. Several small lacrimal ducts carry them onto the eye's surface. Each blink spreads the film across the cornea, where tears bathe, protect and clean the eye and keep it moist.

check.q: In which corner of the orbit does the lacrimal gland lie?
check.a: The superolateral corner.

steps.title: Where tears go
steps.text: Tears drift toward the medial corner, enter two tiny openings on the lid margins and pass along the lacrimal canaliculi into the lacrimal sac. From there the nasolacrimal duct runs down to the nasal cavity, opening under the inferior concha - which is why crying makes your nose run.

check.q: Put in order: lacrimal sac, lacrimal gland, nasolacrimal duct, canaliculi.
check.a: Lacrimal gland -> lacrimal canaliculi -> lacrimal sac -> nasolacrimal duct (-> nasal cavity).

steps.title: The four recti
steps.text: Six extrinsic eye muscles run from the back of the orbit to the eyeball and give quick, precise movements. Four are straight: the superior rectus turns the eye up, the inferior rectus down, the medial rectus in toward the nose and the lateral rectus out.

check.q: Which rectus turns the eye toward the nose?
check.a: The medial rectus.

steps.title: The two obliques
steps.text: The superior oblique runs forward along the medial orbital wall, passes through a fibrous pulley, the trochlea, and turns back to the eyeball; it turns the eye down and out. The inferior oblique runs under the eye from the medial orbital floor and turns it up and out.

check.q: Which muscle's tendon passes through the trochlea, and where does it turn the eye?
check.a: The superior oblique; down and out (inferiorly and laterally).

steps.title: Three nerves: LR6 SO4, rest 3
steps.text:
The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (VI), which 'abducts' the eye. The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (IV), named for its pulley. All the others - superior, inferior and medial rectus, inferior oblique (and levator palpebrae) - get the oculomotor nerve (III).

Following a moving finger, both eyes should track smoothly together; jerky tracking is abnormal.
steps.mnemonic: LR6 SO4, rest 3: lateral rectus - VI, superior oblique - IV, the rest - III.
steps.clinical: In an abducens palsy the affected eye cannot turn outward and drifts inward, giving double vision on looking to that side.

check.q: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus, and which the superior oblique?
check.a: Lateral rectus: abducens (VI). Superior oblique: trochlear (IV).

practice.q: Put the tear pathway in order
The inferior oblique turns the eye
practice.why: Superior oblique: down and out. Inferior oblique: up and out.

practice.q: Which nerve supplies the medial rectus?
practice.why: LR6 SO4, rest 3.

practice.q: A patient cannot turn the right eye outward. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
practice.why: The abducens supplies the lateral rectus, the only muscle that purely abducts the eye.

practice.q: What do tears do for the eye?
practice.a: They bathe, moisten, protect and clean its surface.

practice.q: What should visual tracking of a moving object look like normally?
practice.a: Smooth and coordinated in both eyes; jerky movement is abnormal.

title: Tunics and chambers of the eyeball
summary: Three coats, three chambers, two humors and a lens: the eyeball from outside in.
objectives: Name the three tunics of the eye and the parts of each
Describe the anterior, posterior and vitreous chambers and what fills them
Trace aqueous humor from the ciliary processes to the scleral venous sinus
Describe the lens, its capsule and the suspensory ligaments, and the iris muscles
takeaways: Fibrous tunic = sclera + cornea. Vascular tunic (uvea) = choroid + ciliary body + iris. Nervous tunic = retina.
The cornea is transparent, avascular and does most of the light bending; the sclera protects, anchors the extrinsic muscles and helps hold intraocular pressure.
Anterior chamber (cornea-iris) and posterior chamber (iris-lens) hold aqueous humor: made by the ciliary processes, drained by the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm).
The vitreous chamber behind the lens holds jelly-like vitreous humor that keeps the eyeball's shape and presses the retina against the wall.
Sphincter pupillae (circular, parasympathetic) constricts the pupil; dilator pupillae (radial, sympathetic) dilates it.

steps.title: The fibrous tunic: sclera and cornea
steps.text: The outer coat is the fibrous tunic. Most of it is the white sclera, which protects the eye, gives the extrinsic muscles something to pull on and helps maintain intraocular pressure - the pressure that keeps the eyeball in shape and holds the retina against its wall. At the front it becomes the transparent cornea: dense connective tissue with no blood vessels, an outer epithelium and an inner endothelium. The cornea does most of the eye's refraction.

check.q: Which two structures form the fibrous tunic, and which one bends light most?
check.a: Sclera and cornea; the cornea does most of the refraction.

steps.title: The vascular tunic: choroid, ciliary body, iris
steps.text: The middle coat, the vascular tunic or uvea, has three parts. The choroid is pigmented and full of vessels: it nourishes the eye and its pigment soaks up stray light. Forward, it thickens into the ciliary body - the ciliary muscle, the ciliary ring and the folded ciliary processes. In front is the iris, coloured by melanin; lightly pigmented blue or grey eyes are more sensitive to UV than brown ones.

check.q: Name the three parts of the vascular tunic.
check.a: Choroid, ciliary body and iris.

steps.title: The pupil muscles
steps.text: The iris holds two smooth muscles. The sphincter pupillae is a ring around the pupil; supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve, it constricts the pupil in bright light. The dilator pupillae runs radially like spokes; supplied by sympathetic fibres, it dilates the pupil in dim light (and in fright).

check.q: Which iris muscle constricts the pupil, and which division of the autonomic system drives it?
check.a: The sphincter pupillae (circular), driven by parasympathetic fibres.

steps.title: Chambers and humors
steps.text:
In front of the lens the anterior segment holds aqueous humor in two chambers: the anterior chamber (cornea to iris) and the posterior chamber (iris to lens). The ciliary processes make a few millilitres a day; it flows through the pupil and drains at the angle into the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm).

Behind the lens is the vitreous chamber, filled with jelly-like vitreous humor that keeps the eyeball's shape. Its back wall, seen through the pupil, is the fundus.
steps.clinical: If drainage through the canal of Schlemm is impaired, intraocular pressure rises (glaucoma) and slowly damages the optic nerve.

check.q: Trace aqueous humor from where it is made to where it drains.
check.a: Ciliary processes -> posterior chamber -> pupil -> anterior chamber -> scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm).

steps.title: Lens, retina and the dissected eye
steps.text:
The lens is a disc of clear crystalline protein inside a capsule, hung from the ciliary body by suspensory ligaments (zonular fibres). Lining the back is the retina, the nervous tunic: an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural layer. The central retinal artery and vein enter with the optic nerve.

In a preserved sheep or cow eye the lens is opaque and the retina peels away easily, revealing an iridescent layer of the choroid, the tapetum lucidum, which reflects light back through the retina - the source of 'eye shine' and good night vision. Humans lack it.

check.q: What is the tapetum lucidum, and do humans have one?
check.a: A reflective layer of the choroid in many mammals that bounces light back through the retina (eye shine); humans do not have one.

practice.q: Which is NOT part of the vascular tunic (uvea)?
practice.why: The sclera belongs to the fibrous tunic with the cornea.

practice.q: Aqueous humor is produced by the
practice.why: It is secreted into the posterior chamber and drains via the canal of Schlemm.

practice.q: The posterior chamber lies between the
practice.why: The anterior chamber is between cornea and iris; behind the lens is the vitreous chamber.

practice.q: The dilator pupillae is supplied by
practice.why: Sympathetic: dilate. Parasympathetic: constrict.

practice.q: What does intraocular pressure do?
practice.a: Keeps the eyeball in shape and holds the retina against the posterior wall.

practice.q: What gives the iris its colour?
practice.a: Melanin pigment.

practice.q: What are the two layers of the retina?
practice.a: An outer pigmented layer and an inner neural layer.

title: The retina, photoreceptors and the fundus
summary: Why light passes through the retina backwards, what rods and cones each do, and what an ophthalmoscope shows at the back of the eye.
objectives: Name the retinal layers from the choroid inward and trace light and signal through them
Compare rods and cones
Locate the macula lutea, fovea centralis and optic disc and explain the blind spot
Describe the ophthalmoscope and what a fundus examination can reveal
takeaways: From the choroid inward: pigmented epithelium, rods and cones, bipolar cells, ganglion cells, then the vitreous.
Light crosses the ganglion and bipolar layers to reach the photoreceptors; the signal then runs back: photoreceptor -> bipolar -> ganglion -> optic nerve.
Rods: dim light, black and white, peripheral, more numerous. Cones: colour and acuity, concentrated centrally.
The fovea centralis in the macula lutea is pure cones with the other layers pushed aside - sharpest vision.
The optic disc has no photoreceptors: the blind spot. Fundus examination shows disc, macula and vessels, and can reveal diabetic retinopathy.

steps.title: Layers of the retina
steps.text:
Going inward from the choroid, the retina has a pigmented epithelium, the layer of photoreceptors (rods and cones), the bipolar cell layer and the ganglion cell layer, whose axons run across the inner surface to the optic disc and leave as the optic nerve.

Light enters from the vitreous side and passes through ganglion and bipolar layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back. The signal then travels the other way: photoreceptor, bipolar neuron, ganglion cell.

check.q: In what order does a visual signal pass through the retinal neurons?
check.a: Photoreceptor (rod or cone) -> bipolar neuron -> ganglion cell -> optic nerve.

steps.title: Rods and cones
steps.text:
Rods are far more numerous and very sensitive: they work in dim light and give shape and black-and-white vision. They dominate the peripheral retina. Cones need brighter light and give colour vision and fine visual acuity; they are concentrated centrally.

So an object moving into the edge of your vision is detected (by rods) before you can name its colour (which needs cones).

check.q: Why can you detect an object at the edge of your visual field before you can tell its colour?
check.a: The peripheral retina is rich in rods (sensitive, no colour) and poor in cones (colour).

steps.title: Macula and fovea
steps.text: At the posterior pole, in line with the visual axis, is a yellowish spot, the macula lutea. In its centre is a small pit, the fovea centralis: here the cones are packed most densely and the overlying bipolar and ganglion layers are pushed aside so light falls straight on them. It gives the sharpest vision. When you look intently at something, you turn your eyes so its image lands on the fovea.

check.q: Why is vision sharpest at the fovea centralis?
check.a: It has the highest density of cones and the inner retinal layers are displaced, so light reaches the cones directly.

steps.title: The optic disc and blind spot
steps.text: A little medial (nasal) to the macula, the ganglion cell axons gather and leave the eye as the optic nerve, and the central retinal artery and vein enter and exit. This spot, the optic disc, has no photoreceptors, so light falling on it is not seen: the blind spot. You don't notice it because the other eye and the brain fill the gap.

check.q: Why is the optic disc a blind spot?
check.a: It contains no rods or cones - only exiting nerve fibres and the retinal vessels.

steps.title: Looking in: the ophthalmoscope
steps.text:
An ophthalmoscope shines light through the pupil so you can see the fundus. It has a viewing aperture, a lens selection disc to focus (positive numbers are convex lenses, negative are concave, 0 is no lens), a rheostat to set brightness and a handle holding the battery.

In the fundus you see the pale optic disc, the darker macula with the fovea, and the retinal arteries and veins - the only vessels in the body you can look at directly. Changes in them can reveal systemic disease such as diabetes mellitus.
steps.clinical: In diabetic retinopathy damaged retinal capillaries leak and bleed, and fragile new vessels grow; it is a leading cause of blindness, which is why people with diabetes have regular fundus checks.

check.q: On an ophthalmoscope's lens disc, what do positive and negative numbers mean?
check.a: Positive = convex (converging) lenses; negative = concave (diverging) lenses; 0 = no lens.

practice.q: Order the retinal layers from the choroid inward
Which photoreceptors work best in dim light?
practice.why: Rods are highly sensitive but give no colour.

practice.q: The region of sharpest vision is the
practice.why: Densest cones, overlying layers displaced.

practice.q: The axons of which cells form the optic nerve?
practice.why: Ganglion cell axons converge on the optic disc.

practice.q: A fundus examination can reveal
practice.why: The retinal vessels show the effects of diabetes and hypertension directly.

practice.q: Name the four parts of an ophthalmoscope.
practice.a: Viewing aperture, lens selection disc, rheostat (brightness) control, handle.

practice.q: Why is the blind spot not noticed in everyday vision?
practice.a: The two eyes' blind spots fall on different parts of the scene, and the brain fills in the gap.

title: Focusing, acuity and refractive errors
summary: How the lens changes shape for near vision, why that fails with age, and how acuity, myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism are measured and corrected.
objectives: Explain accommodation in terms of the ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments and lens
Define the near point and presbyopia
Interpret Snellen fractions such as 20/20, 20/15 and 20/100
Explain myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism and how each is corrected
takeaways: Refraction is the bending of light; the cornea bends most, the lens fine-tunes.
Near vision: ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory ligaments slacken, the elastic lens rounds up. Distance: muscle relaxes, ligaments pull taut, lens flattens.
Near point = the closest distance you can focus: about 8-10 cm at 10 years, 80-100 cm at 65. Presbyopia (stiffening lens) shows at 40-50.
Snellen 20/X: you read at 20 ft what a normal eye reads at X ft. 20/15 is better than normal, 20/100 worse.
Myopia: long eye, focus in front of the retina, concave (-) lens. Hyperopia: short eye, focus behind, convex (+) lens. Astigmatism: uneven curvature of cornea or lens.

steps.title: Refraction and accommodation
steps.text: To form a sharp image, light must be bent - refraction - so that it converges on the retina. The cornea does most of the bending; the lens adjusts it. For a distant object the ciliary muscle is relaxed, the suspensory ligaments are taut and pull the lens flat. For a near object the ciliary muscle contracts, the ligaments slacken, and the elastic lens rounds up, bending light more. This is accommodation.
steps.pitfall: The ciliary muscle CONTRACTS for near vision - which slackens the ligaments and lets the lens round up. It is easy to get the direction backwards.

check.q: What do the ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments and lens do when you look at something close?
check.a: The ciliary muscle contracts, the ligaments slacken and the lens becomes rounder.

steps.title: Near point and presbyopia
steps.text:
The near point is the closest distance at which an object can be held in focus. It depends on how elastic the lens is. At about 10 years it is 8-10 cm; by 65 it has receded to 80-100 cm.

As the lens stiffens with age it cannot round up enough for close work: presbyopia. It usually becomes noticeable between 40 and 50, when reading glasses (convex lenses) are needed.

check.q: Why does the near point move further away with age?
check.a: The lens loses elasticity, so it cannot round up enough to focus close objects (presbyopia).

steps.title: Visual acuity: the Snellen chart
steps.text: Visual acuity is sharpness of vision. It is tested with a Snellen chart read from 20 feet, one eye at a time. The result is a fraction: 20/20 is normal. 20/15 means you can read at 20 ft what a normal eye reads only at 15 ft - better than normal. 20/100 means you need to be at 20 ft to read what a normal eye reads at 100 ft - poor acuity.

check.q: What does a Snellen result of 20/40 mean?
check.a: At 20 ft you read what a person with normal vision reads at 40 ft - worse than normal.

steps.title: Myopia and hyperopia
steps.text: In myopia (nearsightedness) the eyeball is too long (or the optics too strong): distant objects focus in front of the retina and look blurred. A concave lens (minus diopters) spreads the light first. In hyperopia (farsightedness) the eyeball is too short: the focus falls behind the retina and near objects blur most. A convex lens (plus diopters) corrects it. The diopter is the unit of lens power.

check.q: A nearsighted eye: where is the focus, what shape is the eyeball, and what lens corrects it?
check.a: In front of the retina; too long; a concave (minus-diopter) lens.

steps.title: Astigmatism
steps.text: A normal cornea is curved evenly, like part of a ball. In astigmatism the cornea (or lens) is curved more steeply in one direction than the other, like the back of a spoon, so lines at some orientations focus sharply and others blur. On an astigmatism chart of lines radiating like a clock face, some lines look darker and crisper than the rest. It is corrected by lenses curved differently in different meridians.

check.q: What causes astigmatism, and what does it do on a radial line chart?
check.a: Unequal curvature of the cornea or lens; lines in some orientations look sharp while others look blurred.

practice.q: Put the events of accommodation for near vision in order
items: Near object focuses on the retina

practice.q: When viewing a distant object the lens is
practice.why: The ciliary muscle relaxes, the ligaments tighten and flatten the lens.

practice.q: A Snellen result of 20/15 means
practice.why: You see at 20 ft what a normal eye sees only at 15 ft.

practice.q: Hyperopia is corrected with
practice.why: The short eye focuses behind the retina; a converging lens brings the focus forward.

practice.q: In myopia the image of a distant object falls
practice.why: The eyeball is too long for its optics.

practice.q: Presbyopia is due to
choices: loss of lens elasticity with age
practice.why: The stiff lens cannot round up for near vision.

practice.q: Define the near point and give typical values at 10 and at 65 years.
practice.a: The closest distance at which an object can be held in focus: about 8-10 cm at 10, 80-100 cm at 65.

practice.q: What is a diopter?
practice.a: The unit of lens power; + for convex (converging), - for concave (diverging).

practice.q: What is refraction?
practice.a: The bending of light as it passes between media such as air, cornea and lens.

title: Visual pathway, visual fields and pupil reflexes
summary: From retina to occipital cortex: which fibres cross at the chiasm, why each hemisphere sees the opposite field, binocular vision, and the pupillary light reflex.
objectives: Trace the visual pathway from the optic nerve to the primary visual cortex
Explain which retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm and why each hemisphere sees the opposite visual field
Relate visual field overlap to binocular (stereoscopic) vision and depth perception
Describe the direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes and their nerves
takeaways: Optic nerve -> optic chiasm -> optic tract -> lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus -> optic radiation -> primary visual cortex (occipital lobe).
At the chiasm nasal retinal fibres cross; temporal fibres stay on the same side. Each hemisphere therefore sees the opposite visual field.
The nasal part of each visual field falls on the temporal retina and vice versa.
Overlap of the two fields gives binocular, stereoscopic vision and depth perception; prey animals trade overlap for wide fields.
Light in one eye constricts both pupils (direct and consensual): in via CN II, out via parasympathetic fibres in CN III to the sphincter pupillae.

steps.title: Retina to cortex
steps.text: Ganglion cell axons leave each eye as the optic nerve. The two nerves meet at the optic chiasm in front of the pituitary, and continue as the optic tracts around the brainstem to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. From there the optic radiations fan back to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, lining the calcarine sulcus. Further processing, such as recognising objects, happens in the temporal lobe.

check.q: List the visual pathway from optic nerve to cortex.
check.a: Optic nerve -> optic chiasm -> optic tract -> lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) -> optic radiation -> primary visual cortex (occipital lobe).

steps.title: Crossing at the chiasm
steps.text:
The lens inverts the image, so the nasal half of each visual field lands on the temporal retina and the temporal field on the nasal retina. At the chiasm only the fibres from the nasal (medial) retina cross; temporal retinal fibres stay on the same side.

Result: the left optic tract carries everything seen in the right visual field by both eyes, so each hemisphere sees the opposite (contralateral) visual field.
steps.clinical: A pituitary tumour pressing up on the chiasm damages the crossing nasal fibres and knocks out both temporal visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).

check.q: The right optic tract is cut. Which visual field is lost?
check.a: The left visual field of both eyes (the right tract carries right temporal and left nasal retinal fibres).

steps.title: Visual fields and depth
steps.text:
The visual field is everything one eye can see while it is held still. The two fields overlap in the middle; the degree of overlap gives binocular (stereoscopic) vision: each eye sees the object from a slightly different angle and the brain turns the difference into depth perception.

Prey animals, with eyes on the sides of the head, have huge total fields but little overlap. Predators, birds of prey and tree-dwellers, with forward-facing eyes, trade field width for stereoscopic vision.

check.q: What gives depth perception, and which kind of animal has more of it?
check.a: Overlap of the two visual fields (binocular, stereoscopic vision); predators with forward-facing eyes.

steps.title: Pupillary light reflexes
steps.text: Pupils constrict in bright light and dilate in dim light. Shine a light in one eye and that pupil constricts - the direct reflex - and the other pupil constricts at the same time - the consensual reflex. The afferent limb is the optic nerve (II); the efferent limb is parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve (III) to the sphincter pupillae. Both sides are wired to both, so both pupils respond.

check.q: Light shone in the left eye makes the right pupil constrict. What is this called, and which nerves are involved?
check.a: The consensual light reflex; afferent optic nerve (II), efferent parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve (III).

steps.title: The superior colliculi
steps.text: Not every optic tract fibre goes to the thalamus. Some leave for the superior colliculi of the midbrain (and the nearby pretectal area), which drive visual reflexes: turning the eyes and head toward a sudden movement, and the pupillary light reflex. That is why a reflex can survive damage to the visual cortex.

check.q: What do the superior colliculi do with visual input?
check.a: They drive visual reflexes, such as turning the eyes and head toward a moving stimulus.

practice.q: Put the visual pathway in order
At the optic chiasm, which fibres cross?
choices: Those from the nasal half of each retina
Those from the temporal half of each retina
practice.why: Temporal fibres stay ipsilateral.

practice.q: The left occipital cortex receives information about
practice.why: Each hemisphere sees the contralateral visual field.

practice.q: The nasal part of the visual field falls on the
practice.why: The lens inverts and reverses the image.

practice.q: The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is
choices: parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve
practice.why: CN III parasympathetics supply the sphincter pupillae.

practice.q: What is the consensual light reflex?
practice.a: Constriction of the pupil of the unlit eye when light is shone into the other eye.

practice.q: Why do owls and cats have better depth perception than rabbits?
practice.a: Their forward-facing eyes give a large overlap of the visual fields (binocular vision); rabbits' side eyes give wide fields with little overlap.

title: Colour vision, photopigments and afterimages
summary: Three kinds of cone, why red-green colour blindness is mostly male, and what bleaching of rhodopsin has to do with afterimages.
objectives: Name the three cone types and explain how they give colour vision
Explain the inheritance of red-green colour blindness and how it is tested
Describe rhodopsin and bleaching
Explain positive and negative afterimages
takeaways: Three cone types are most sensitive to red (long), green (medium) and blue (short) wavelengths; colour is read from their relative activity.
Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive: one copy affects a male (XY); females are usually carriers. It is screened with Ishihara plates or yarn matching.
Some people lack a cone type entirely; others have one with reduced sensitivity.
Rhodopsin (visual purple) = opsin + retinal, a vitamin A derivative. Light splits it - bleaching.
Positive afterimage: photoreceptors keep firing briefly. Negative afterimage: bleached receptors are fatigued, so unbleached ones dominate and the image appears reversed.

steps.title: Three kinds of cone
steps.text: Colour vision depends on three types of cone, most sensitive to long (red), medium (green) and short (blue) wavelengths. Their sensitivities overlap, and the brain reads colour from the ratio of their activity: yellow light, for example, stimulates red and green cones about equally.

check.q: Which three cone types are there?
check.a: Red-sensitive (long wavelength), green-sensitive (medium) and blue-sensitive (short).

steps.title: Colour blindness
steps.text:
The common red-green colour blindness comes from genes on the X chromosome and is X-linked recessive. A male (XY) with one affected X is colour blind; a female needs two, so she is usually an unaffected carrier. Some people lack one cone type entirely; more have a cone type with reduced sensitivity and confuse only some shades.

It is screened with Ishihara plates - numbers made of coloured dots hidden in dots of another colour - or by matching coloured yarns.

check.q: Why is red-green colour blindness much more common in males?
check.a: It is X-linked recessive; males have one X, so a single affected copy shows, whereas females with one copy are carriers.

steps.title: Rhodopsin and bleaching
steps.text: Rods contain rhodopsin (visual purple), made of a protein, opsin, bound to retinal, a light-absorbing molecule derived from vitamin A. When light strikes it, rhodopsin splits into retinal and opsin - bleaching - and that change starts the electrical signal. It must be rebuilt before the rod can respond fully again. Cones use similar pigments with different opsins.
steps.clinical: Vitamin A deficiency limits retinal supply, so rods recover slowly: night blindness is its earliest sign.

check.q: What are the two components of rhodopsin, and what happens to it in light?
check.a: Opsin and retinal (from vitamin A); light splits them apart - bleaching.

steps.title: Afterimages
steps.text:
Stare at a bright image and look away. For a moment you may still see it in its own colours: a positive afterimage, because the photoreceptors keep firing briefly after the stimulus stops.

Then a reversed image appears - light where it was dark, and in complementary colours: a negative afterimage. The receptors that were stimulated are bleached and fatigued, so the unbleached ones around them signal more strongly.

check.q: Why is a negative afterimage reversed?
check.a: The receptors that saw the bright parts are bleached and fatigued, so unbleached receptors signal relatively more.

practice.q: Red-green colour blindness is inherited as
practice.why: The cone opsin genes involved are on the X chromosome.

practice.q: A woman with one affected X chromosome for red-green colour blindness is usually
choices: a carrier with normal colour vision
practice.why: Her other X usually provides a normal gene.

practice.q: Retinal, part of rhodopsin, is made from
practice.why: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.

practice.q: Light splitting rhodopsin into retinal and opsin is called
practice.why: The pigment loses its purple colour.

practice.q: A negative afterimage appears because
practice.why: A positive afterimage is due to continued firing; a negative one to fatigue.

practice.q: What is an Ishihara plate?
practice.a: A pattern of coloured dots containing a number that people with a colour deficiency cannot see (or see differently).

practice.q: What is rhodopsin also called, and where is it found?
practice.a: Visual purple; in the rods.

title: The external and middle ear
summary: From the auricle to the oval window: how sound is funnelled, turned into eardrum movement and amplified by three tiny bones.
objectives: Name the three regions of the ear and the parts of the external ear
Name the ossicles, their ligaments and the two middle-ear muscles
Explain how the middle ear amplifies sound about 20 times
Describe the auditory tube, its job and its role in middle ear infection
takeaways: External ear = auricle (pinna) + external acoustic meatus, ending at the tympanic membrane.
The helix is elastic cartilage covered by skin (stratified squamous epithelium); the lobule has no cartilage.
Malleus (on the eardrum) -> incus -> stapes (footplate in the oval window), slung by the superior and anterior ligaments of the malleus and the posterior ligament of the incus.
A large eardrum driving a small oval window amplifies pressure about 20x; tensor tympani and stapedius damp loud sounds.
The auditory tube links the middle ear to the nasopharynx, equalises pressure, and lets infection in (otitis media, especially in children).

steps.title: Three regions of the ear
steps.text: The ear has an external ear that collects sound, an air-filled middle ear that transmits it, and a fluid-filled inner ear that turns it into nerve impulses and also senses balance. The middle and inner ear are hollowed out of the temporal bone.

check.q: Which region of the ear is air-filled and which fluid-filled?
check.a: The middle ear is air-filled; the inner ear is fluid-filled.

steps.title: Auricle, meatus and eardrum
steps.text: The auricle (pinna) funnels sound into the ear. Its rim is the helix, a fold of elastic cartilage covered by skin - stratified squamous epithelium; the soft lobule (earlobe) has no cartilage. The external acoustic meatus runs into the temporal bone and ends at the tympanic membrane (eardrum): thin connective tissue covered by epithelium on both sides. It marks the border with the middle ear and vibrates with incoming sound pressure waves.

check.q: What tissue supports the helix?
check.a: Elastic cartilage, covered by skin.

steps.title: The ossicles
steps.text: Across the tympanic cavity runs a chain of three bones, the auditory ossicles. The malleus (hammer) has its handle attached to the eardrum; its head articulates with the incus (anvil), which passes the movement to the stapes (stirrup), whose footplate sits in the oval window of the inner ear. Small ligaments hang the chain in place: the superior and anterior ligaments of the malleus and the posterior ligament of the incus.

check.q: Name the ossicles in order from eardrum to inner ear.
check.a: Malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), stapes (stirrup).

steps.title: Amplification and protection
steps.text: Fluid is much harder to move than air. The middle ear solves this by concentrating force: the large tympanic membrane drives the tiny oval window, raising the pressure about 20 times. Two small muscles protect the inner ear from loud sound by stiffening the chain: tensor tympani, on the malleus, and stapedius, on the stapes. The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve carrying taste, crosses the middle ear between malleus and incus.

check.q: How does the middle ear amplify sound, and by roughly how much?
check.a: The large eardrum drives the small oval window, concentrating the force - about 20x pressure gain.

steps.title: The auditory tube
steps.text:
The auditory (pharyngotympanic, Eustachian) tube runs from the middle ear down and forward to the nasopharynx. Opening it when you swallow or yawn equalises pressure on the two sides of the eardrum - the 'pop' when a plane descends.

It is also a route for throat infections to reach the middle ear: otitis media. In children the tube is shorter and more horizontal, so they get it far more often.

check.q: Why are children more prone to otitis media?
check.a: Their auditory tube is shorter and more horizontal, so infection spreads easily from the nasopharynx.

practice.q: Put the path of sound in order
Which ossicle is attached to the tympanic membrane?
practice.why: The handle of the malleus is embedded in the eardrum.

practice.q: The stapedius muscle attaches to the
practice.why: Tensor tympani is on the malleus; stapedius on the stapes.

practice.q: The auditory tube connects the middle ear with the
practice.why: It equalises pressure and can carry infection from the throat.

practice.q: What is the job of tensor tympani and stapedius?
practice.a: They stiffen the ossicular chain to damp loud sounds and protect the inner ear.

practice.q: What epithelium covers the auricle?
practice.a: Stratified squamous epithelium (skin).

title: The inner ear and the cochlea
summary: Two labyrinths, two fluids, three scalae and a spiral organ that sorts sound by pitch along its length.
objectives: Distinguish the bony and membranous labyrinths and their fluids
Name the three regions of the inner ear and their functions, and the roles of the oval and round windows
Identify the three scalae, the vestibular, basilar and tectorial membranes and the spiral organ
Explain how hair cells transduce sound and how the basilar membrane sorts pitch
takeaways: Bony labyrinth (lined by endosteum) holds perilymph; the membranous labyrinth inside it holds endolymph.
Cochlea - hearing; vestibule - static balance and linear acceleration; semicircular canals - rotation.
The stapes pushes the oval window; the round window bulges out to let the cochlear fluid move.
Scala vestibuli and scala tympani (perilymph) meet at the helicotrema; the cochlear duct (endolymph) lies between, bounded by the vestibular and basilar membranes.

The spiral organ sits on the basilar membrane: inner and outer hair cells whose stereocilia touch the tectorial membrane. Base = narrow, stiff, high pitch (to 20,000 Hz); apex = wide, floppy, low pitch (to 20 Hz).

steps.title: Two labyrinths, two fluids
steps.text:
The inner ear is a set of tunnels in the petrous temporal bone, the bony labyrinth, lined by endosteum and filled with perilymph, a fluid like CSF; fine fibrous strands from perilymphatic cells cross it and tether the soft tubes inside. Inside it lies a matching set of soft tubes and sacs, the membranous labyrinth, filled with endolymph.

It has three regions: the cochlea for hearing, the vestibule for static balance and linear acceleration, and the semicircular canals for rotation.

check.q: Which fluid fills the bony labyrinth and which the membranous labyrinth?
check.a: Perilymph in the bony labyrinth; endolymph in the membranous labyrinth.

steps.title: Oval and round windows
steps.text: Two openings join the middle and inner ear. The oval window holds the footplate of the stapes: each inward push sends a pressure wave through the perilymph of the cochlea. Fluid cannot be compressed, so something must give: the membrane-covered round window bulges outward into the middle ear, relieving the pressure and letting the fluid move.

check.q: Why does the inner ear need a round window?
check.a: Perilymph is incompressible; the round window bulges out so the fluid can move when the stapes pushes in.

steps.title: Three scalae
steps.text: Cut across a turn of the cochlea and you see three channels. On top is the scala vestibuli and at the bottom the scala tympani, both full of perilymph and joined at the apex through the helicotrema. Between them is the cochlear duct (scala media), full of endolymph. It is separated from the scala vestibuli by the thin vestibular membrane and from the scala tympani by the basilar membrane, which stretches from the bony spiral lamina to the spiral ligament on the outer wall.

check.q: Which membrane separates the cochlear duct from the scala tympani?
check.a: The basilar membrane (the vestibular membrane separates it from the scala vestibuli).

steps.title: The spiral organ
steps.text:
On the basilar membrane sits the spiral organ (organ of Corti): one row of inner hair cells, three rows of outer hair cells, and supporting cells. The stereocilia of the hair cells are embedded in the overhanging tectorial membrane.

Sound makes the basilar membrane vibrate relative to the tectorial membrane, the stereocilia bend, the hair cells depolarise and release transmitter, and nerve endings of the cochlear nerve fire. Their cell bodies form the cochlear (spiral) ganglion.

check.q: What bends the stereocilia of cochlear hair cells?
check.a: Movement of the basilar membrane relative to the tectorial membrane in which they are embedded.

steps.title: Pitch and place: tonotopy
steps.text: Humans hear about 20 to 20,000 Hz (cycles per second). The basilar membrane changes along its length: at the base, near the oval window, it is narrow (about 0.04 mm) and stiff and vibrates best to high frequencies; at the apex, by the helicotrema, it is wide (about 0.5 mm) and floppy and responds to low frequencies. Each pitch therefore excites its own place, and the brain reads pitch from which hair cells fire: tonotopy.
steps.clinical: Hair cells at the base take the first beating from loud noise and age, so high frequencies are usually lost first.

check.q: Where along the cochlea are high frequencies detected, and why there?
check.a: At the base, near the oval window, where the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff.

practice.q: Endolymph fills the
practice.why: The cochlear duct is part of the membranous labyrinth.

practice.q: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani connect at the
practice.why: The helicotrema is at the apex of the cochlea.

practice.q: Low-frequency sounds maximally vibrate the basilar membrane
practice.why: The apex is wide and floppy.

practice.q: Which part of the inner ear senses rotation?
practice.why: The vestibule senses static position and linear acceleration.

practice.q: What is the human hearing range?
practice.a: About 20 to 20,000 Hz.

practice.q: Name the three kinds of cell in the spiral organ.
practice.a: Inner hair cells (one row), outer hair cells (three rows) and supporting cells.

practice.q: Order the events of sound transduction
items: Stereocilia bend against the tectorial membrane

title: The auditory pathway and hearing tests
summary: From cochlear nerve to auditory cortex, and how audiometry and the Weber and Rinne tests tell conduction deafness from sensorineural deafness.
objectives: Trace the auditory pathway from the cochlear nerve to the auditory cortex
Explain how an audiometer measures hearing threshold and what counts as significant loss
Distinguish conduction from sensorineural deafness and give causes of each
Predict Weber and Rinne results for normal hearing and each type of loss
takeaways: Cochlear nerve -> cochlear nuclei (brainstem) -> superior olivary nucleus -> inferior colliculus -> medial geniculate nucleus (thalamus) -> auditory cortex (temporal lobe).
The superior olivary nucleus gets input from both ears and localises sound; reflex fibres go to tensor tympani and stapedius.
Threshold = the softest sound heard in at least half of trials, in decibels, at 125-8000 Hz; loss is significant at >= 20 dB at two frequencies or >= 30 dB at one.
Conduction deafness: sound does not reach the cochlea (wax, perforated drum, otitis media, otosclerosis). Sensorineural: hair cells, cochlear nerve or auditory cortex damaged.
Weber: louder in the bad ear with conductive loss, in the good ear with sensorineural loss. Rinne: air > bone is normal; bone > air (negative Rinne) means conductive loss.

steps.title: The auditory pathway
steps.text: The cochlear nerve (part of CN VIII) enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction and synapses in the cochlear nuclei. From there signals go to the superior olivary nucleus, which receives input from both ears and compares them to localise sound; it also sends reflex fibres to the nerves of tensor tympani and stapedius. The pathway climbs to the inferior colliculus, the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and finally the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

check.q: Why can one ear alone not localise sound well?
check.a: Localisation depends on comparing the two ears (timing and loudness) in the superior olivary nucleus.

steps.title: Audiometry
steps.text:
An audiometer plays pure tones from 125 to 8000 Hz at controlled loudness, measured in decibels (dB). For each frequency the hearing threshold is the softest tone heard in at least half of the trials, and the results are plotted as an audiogram.

Hearing loss is significant when the threshold is raised by 20 dB or more at two frequencies, or 30 dB or more at one.

check.q: How is a hearing threshold defined on an audiometer?
check.a: The lowest intensity (dB) at which a tone is heard in at least 50% of presentations.

steps.title: Two kinds of deafness
steps.text:
In conduction deafness sound fails to reach the cochlea: the meatus is blocked with earwax, the eardrum is perforated, the middle ear is full of fluid (otitis media) or the stapes is fixed by bone (otosclerosis). The inner ear itself is fine.

In sensorineural deafness the problem is in the hair cells, the cochlear nerve or the auditory cortex.

check.q: Is deafness from a perforated eardrum conductive or sensorineural?
check.a: Conductive.

steps.title: Weber and Rinne tests
steps.text:
Both use a 256 Hz tuning fork. Weber: the fork is placed on the forehead (bone conduction). Normally it is heard equally in both ears; with conductive loss it is louder in the bad ear; with sensorineural loss, louder in the good ear.

Rinne: the fork is held on the mastoid process until it fades, then beside the meatus (air conduction). Normally air beats bone (positive Rinne). If bone beats air (negative Rinne), there is conductive loss in that ear.

check.q: Weber lateralises to the left ear and the left Rinne is negative. What kind of loss is it, and on which side?
check.a: Conductive hearing loss in the left ear.

steps.title: Age, noise and localisation
steps.text:
Age-related loss, presbycusis, comes from loss of hair cells and a stiffer eardrum and ossicles; the high frequencies go first, and it often comes with tinnitus, ringing in the ears. Noise-induced loss from loud music, headphones, machinery or firearms also destroys hair cells, which do not regrow.

We localise sound by comparing the two ears: the nearer ear hears the sound slightly sooner and louder.

check.q: Which frequencies are lost first in presbycusis, and why?
check.a: High frequencies - hair cells at the base of the cochlea, which detect them, are lost first.

practice.q: Put the auditory pathway in order
Which nucleus compares input from the two ears to localise sound?
practice.why: It is the first site of binaural convergence.

practice.q: In a Weber test with sensorineural loss in the right ear, the sound is
practice.why: The damaged cochlea hears less by any route, so the good ear wins.

practice.q: A negative Rinne (bone louder than air) indicates
practice.why: Air conduction is blocked, so bone conduction dominates.

practice.q: Which is a cause of sensorineural deafness?
practice.why: The others block conduction to a healthy cochlea.

practice.q: Significant hearing loss on an audiogram is a threshold raised by
choices: >= 20 dB at two frequencies or >= 30 dB at one
practice.why: These cut-offs define significant loss.

practice.q: What frequency of tuning fork is used for the Weber and Rinne tests?
What is tinnitus?
practice.a: A ringing or buzzing heard in the ears without an external sound.

practice.q: Name three causes of noise-induced hearing loss.
practice.a: Loud music or headphones, industrial machinery, firearms.

title: Balance: vestibule, semicircular canals and tests
summary: Otoliths for tilt, cupulae for turning, and the reflexes and bedside tests that depend on them.
objectives: Describe the maculae of the utricle and saccule and how they sense head position and linear acceleration
Describe the crista ampullaris and how rotation bends the cupula
Match each semicircular canal to the movement it senses best
Explain the vestibulo-ocular reflex, nystagmus and the Barany and Romberg tests
takeaways: Static labyrinth = vestibule (utricle + saccule). Their maculae hold hair cells under a gelatinous otolithic membrane loaded with calcium carbonate otoliths.
Each hair cell has many stereocilia and one kinocilium; bending them toward the kinocilium excites the vestibular nerve fibre.
Dynamic labyrinth = three semicircular canals at right angles. In each ampulla a crista ampullaris carries hair cells capped by a gelatinous cupula; endolymph lags during rotation and bends it.
Anterior canal: forward-backward (somersault). Posterior: sideways tilt (cartwheel). Lateral: horizontal spin. Combined movements use several canals.

Vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes opposite to the head; post-rotatory nystagmus after spinning (Barany). Romberg: more sway with eyes closed suggests vestibular, proprioceptive or neural dysfunction.

steps.title: The vestibule: utricle and saccule
steps.text: The vestibule holds two sacs of the membranous labyrinth, the utricle and saccule - the static labyrinth. Each has a patch of sensory epithelium, a macula: hair cells and supporting cells covered by a gelatinous otolithic membrane studded with calcium carbonate crystals, the otoliths. Each hair cell has many stereocilia and one tall kinocilium, and is supplied by fibres of the vestibular nerve.

check.q: What are otoliths and where are they?
check.a: Calcium carbonate crystals in the otolithic membrane over the maculae of the utricle and saccule.

steps.title: Static equilibrium
steps.text:
Otoliths are heavier than the fluid around them. Tilt the head, or accelerate in a straight line (linear acceleration) as in a lift or a car, and the otolithic membrane slides, bending the hair cells. This reports the position of the head relative to gravity: static equilibrium.

Balance also uses vision and proprioception. When the eyes and the vestibule disagree - reading in a moving car - the mismatch causes imbalance, nausea and motion sickness.

check.q: Why do you feel carsick when reading in a moving car?
check.a: Your eyes report a still page while the vestibule reports motion; the mismatch causes motion sickness.

steps.title: Semicircular canals and cristae
steps.text:
The three semicircular canals - anterior, posterior and lateral - lie at right angles to one another and hold the endolymph-filled semicircular ducts: the dynamic labyrinth. At the base of each is a swelling, the ampulla, containing a ridge of hair cells, the crista ampullaris, capped by a gelatinous cupula.

When the head starts to turn, the endolymph lags behind through inertia, pushes the cupula over and bends the hair cells: angular (rotational) acceleration is sensed - dynamic equilibrium.

check.q: What bends the cupula when you start to spin?
check.a: The endolymph in the duct lags behind the moving head (inertia) and pushes on the cupula.

steps.title: Which canal for which movement
steps.text: Each canal responds best to rotation in its own plane. The anterior canal senses forward-backward head movement, as in a somersault or nodding. The posterior canal senses sideways tilting, as in a cartwheel. The lateral canal senses horizontal rotation, as in spinning or shaking the head 'no'. Real movements usually combine planes, so more than one canal fires.

check.q: Which canal is most stimulated by spinning on a chair with the head upright?
check.a: The lateral (horizontal) canal.

steps.title: Reflexes and balance tests
steps.text:
The vestibulo-ocular reflex turns the eyes opposite to a head movement so the image stays steady. Barany test: spinning in a chair with the head tilted about 30 degrees forward puts the lateral canals horizontal; when the spin stops the endolymph keeps moving, and the eyes show nystagmus - involuntary, rhythmic twitching.

Postural reflexes use negative feedback to keep us upright. Romberg test: stand with feet together, eyes open and then closed; much more sway with eyes closed (positive Romberg) suggests a problem with the vestibular apparatus, the proprioceptors or their nerve pathways.

check.q: Why does a Romberg test compare eyes open with eyes closed?
check.a: Closing the eyes removes vision, so balance depends on the vestibular system and proprioception; increased sway exposes a problem there.

practice.q: Head tilt is sensed mainly by the
choices: maculae of the utricle and saccule
practice.why: Gravity pulls on the otoliths.

practice.q: The cupula is found in the
practice.why: It caps the crista ampullaris.

practice.q: A cartwheel most stimulates the
practice.why: Anterior: somersault. Posterior: cartwheel. Lateral: spinning.

practice.q: Post-rotatory nystagmus is caused by
choices: endolymph continuing to move after the spin stops
practice.why: The moving endolymph keeps deflecting the cupula.

practice.q: A positive Romberg sign means
choices: increased sway with the eyes closed
practice.why: It points to vestibular, proprioceptive or neural dysfunction.

practice.q: What is the vestibulo-ocular reflex?
practice.a: A reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation to keep the image stable on the retina.

practice.q: What is nystagmus?
practice.a: Involuntary, rhythmic twitching movements of the eyes.

practice.q: Why is the head tilted about 30 degrees forward in the Barany test?
practice.a: It brings the lateral semicircular canals into the horizontal plane of rotation.

practice.q: What is a postural reflex?
practice.a: A negative-feedback reflex that moves the limbs or trunk to restore the centre of balance and keep us upright.
